11. A final conclusion relates to the inescapable interdependence of various groups within the impact area. For example, Crow labor force behavior will be a primary determinant of non-Crow in-migration to Hardin. The timing of the mining plans of one company will affect the nature and extent of the impacts that other companies' mining plans will have. The over-riding conclusion is obvious: if mutually beneficial development is to be achieved, these many interdependencies will have to be recognized, and discussed. They will have to strongly influence the planning and actions which are undertaken to meet the social and economic needs of the impact area.
Impacts on Farmers and Ranchers
There are currently 11 families living in the Sarpy Creek area that raise livestock and grow crops on the lands of Tracts II and III (Westmoreland Resources, 1975 f, p. 244.). Mining will be highly disruptive to the lifestyles of these families due to the preemption of agricultural land uses, the daily influx of people working at the mine, and the change in character of the area from rural to industrial. Social disruptions resulting from relocation of families and disagreements regarding the selling of land have occurred and will continue to occur, although the initial and most severe impact probably already has been felt.
